skills.describe: Characteristics, not a name: what the pattern or process is like, where, and how much
skills.explain: A cause and its effect with every link: because, so, therefore
skills.compare: Both sides of the comparison, in one sentence each or one sentence for both
skills.degree: A stated degree (high, moderate, low), then the evidence for it
skills.place: A named real place, region or country, not "some countries"
skills.scale: The scale of analysis named and used: the scale of the data, not the size of the map
skills.limitation: What the source cannot show, and why
skills.model: How well a named model fits this case, with one limit of the model
skills.legend: Read the legend: the class, the unit and what each shade or symbol stands for, before you say what the map shows

prompts.title: Reading a chart's key
prompts.context: A bar chart shows the share of households with internet access at home in Province X of invented Country A. Its key says the dark bar is 2010 and the light bar is 2020. The dark bar reaches 30% and the light bar 75% (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Describe the change the chart shows in Province X.
checklist: Uses the key to say which bar is which year
Gives both values and the direction of change
Says how large the change is, in points or as a multiple

earns.answer: Using the key, the dark bar is 2010 and the light bar 2020: the share of households with internet at home in Province X rose from 30% in 2010 to 75% in 2020, an increase of 45 percentage points, to two and a half times the share.
earns.why: It reads the key, gives both values in order and says how large the change is.

misses.answer: The light bar is taller, so Province X has more internet now than it did before.
misses.why: It never reads the key or the values, so it cannot say when or how much the share changed.

why.1: The key says the light bar is 2020.
why.2: The chart has no 2015 bar.

why.1: The 2020 bar is taller, so the share rose.
why.2: The two bars differ: 30% and 75%.

prompts.title: Naming the scale of province data
prompts.context: A table gives one value for each of the eight provinces of invented Country A: the share of adults who finished high school (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Identify the scale of analysis of the data, and explain how you can tell.
checklist: Names the local (subnational) scale of analysis
Ties it to the data: one value for each of the provinces
Does not use the size of the area covered as the reason

earns.answer: The data are at the local scale (subnational), because each value in the table is for one province, not one number for the whole of Country A.
earns.why: It names the scale and gives the reason in the data: eight values, one per province.

misses.answer: The national scale, because the table covers the whole of Country A.
misses.why: The table covers the country, but the scale of analysis is the level of the data, and these data are for provinces.

why.1: National data would be one value for the whole country; this table has eight.
why.2: Global data would compare countries of the world; this table is one country.

evidence.label: How you can tell
options: each value is for one province
the table covers the whole country

why.1: That is the area covered, not the level of the data.
why.2: Eight rows are the eight provinces; the point is that each is one province.

prompts.title: Turning a fact into an explanation
prompts.context: A free-response part asks: "Explain one reason a town might grow beside a large river."
prompts.prompt: Write an answer that would earn the point, with the link from the cause to the effect stated.
checklist: Names a cause: what the river offers
States the link with because, so or which leads to
Ends at the effect asked for: the town grows bigger

earns.answer: A large river is an easy route for boats, so goods can be shipped in and out cheaply, which brings trade and jobs to the town, and the town grows as people come for that work.
earns.why: It starts with what the river offers and links each step to the next until the town grows.

misses.answer: Rivers give towns water and an easy route for boats and ships.
misses.why: It lists what rivers give but never says how that makes the town grow: the link is missing.

cause.label: Cause
options: the river is an easy route for boats

why.1: Beauty is not a reason the exam would credit for growth.
why.2: Floods are a hazard that would slow growth, not a reason for it.

link.label: Link
options: so trade and jobs come to the town
rivers are found on most continents

why.1: True of rivers, but it does not tie the river to the town's growth.
why.2: A name explains nothing about growth.

prompts.title: Describing an elevation pattern
prompts.context: An isoline map of invented Country A shows lines of equal height above sea level: 1,500 meters in the Western Uplands, then 1,000, 500 and 100 meters eastward toward the South Coast. The lines are close together in the west and far apart in the east (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Describe the pattern of elevation the map shows.
checklist: Says where the land is highest and where it is lowest, with values
Says which way the land slopes
Uses the spacing of the lines: close lines are steep land

earns.answer: Elevation is highest in the Western Uplands, above 1,500 meters, and falls eastward to below 100 meters near the South Coast. The lines are closest together in the west, so the land is steepest there, and the east is low and gentle.
earns.why: It names where, how high and which way the land slopes, and reads the line spacing as steepness.

misses.answer: The map shows the elevation of Country A with isolines.
misses.why: That names the map type but describes no pattern: no place, no values and no direction.

pattern.label: Where the land is highest
options: the east, where lines are far apart

why.1: The South Coast is the lowest land on the map.
why.2: Far-apart lines mean gentle, lower land.

why.1: Flat land has lines far apart.
why.2: Isolines of height say nothing about people.

prompts.title: Reading a graduated symbol legend
prompts.context: A graduated symbol map shows how many people commute each day into Port Ora, the capital, from each province of invented Country A. The legend shows circles for 10,000, 50,000 and 100,000 commuters, drawn so a circle's area matches its number (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Describe what a circle the size of the middle legend circle in the Central Valley means.
checklist: Reads the value from the legend: about 50,000
Says what is counted: daily commuters into Port Ora
Does not read it as everyone who lives in the province

earns.answer: About 50,000 people commute each day from the Central Valley into Port Ora: the circle's area, matched to the legend, shows the count of commuters, not the share of residents and not the size of the province.
earns.why: It reads the value and the variable from the legend and says what the circle does not show.

misses.answer: Lots of people live in the Central Valley, so its circle is big.
misses.why: The circle counts commuters, not residents, and the answer never reads a number from the legend.

why.1: That is the largest legend circle.
why.2: The legend counts people, not a percent.

why.1: The map shows commuters only.
why.2: Circle size is a count of commuters, not area.

prompts.title: Why satellites suit the Amazon
prompts.context: Brazil's space research agency, INPE, has used satellite images since the 1980s to measure how much of the Amazon rainforest is cleared each year.
prompts.prompt: Explain why satellite images are a good source for tracking forest clearing in the Amazon.
checklist: Names a strength of remote sensing: it covers a huge, remote area
Says it measures the same way each year, so years can be compared
Links that strength to tracking change in the forest

earns.answer: Satellites photograph the whole forest in the same way every year, so analysts can compare one year's cleared area with the last, which lets them measure change across land too large and remote to measure on foot.
earns.why: It names what remote sensing does and links it, with so and which, to tracking change.

misses.answer: Satellites can take pictures of the rainforest from far above the Earth.
misses.why: True, but it does not explain why that makes them a good source for tracking clearing year by year.

cause.label: Strength
options: they cover a huge, remote area the same way each year
they record why each farmer cleared land
they need no experts to read

why.1: Images show where forest is cleared, not the reasons.
why.2: Reading the images takes trained analysts.

effect.label: So what
options: so cleared area can be compared from year to year
so the forest stops being cleared
so maps are no longer needed

why.1: Measuring clearing does not stop it.
why.2: The images are often turned into maps.

prompts.title: The limit of an online questionnaire
prompts.context: The government of Port Ora, the invented capital of Country A, posts an online questionnaire about bus routes, and 2,000 residents answer it (invented for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain one limitation of using this questionnaire to plan bus routes.
checklist: Names who the online questionnaire misses
Explains why that matters for planning bus routes
Says which way the results may be off, and why

earns.answer: The questionnaire reaches only people who go online, so households without internet, often older or poorer residents who may rely most on buses, are left out, and the results can understate their needs.
earns.why: It names who is missed, ties them to bus use and says how the results are biased.

misses.answer: The questionnaire might be wrong because people make mistakes.
misses.why: Too vague: it does not say what the questionnaire misses or why that matters for buses.

limit.label: Who is missed
options: people who live in Port Ora

why.1: Duplicate answers can be removed; the bigger gap is who never sees it.
why.2: Port Ora's residents are the ones it is for.

effect.label: Why it matters
options: they may rely most on buses

why.1: Everyone travels somehow; the point is who depends on buses.
why.2: Car owners rely less on buses.

prompts.title: Naming a place: census data
prompts.context: A student writes: "Governments use census data to make decisions."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim so it names a real place, the data and the decision.
checklist: Names a real place and its census, with a year
Names one decision the data drove
Is more than the general claim

earns.answer: In the United States, the 2020 census counts set how many members each state sends to the House of Representatives, and Texas gained two seats after it.
earns.why: It names the country, the census year, the decision and a specific result.

misses.answer: Governments use census data to decide things like how many seats different places get.
misses.why: No place and no year, so a reader cannot check it or see the data at work.

why.1: "Some country" names no place.
why.2: There is no single world census.

outcome.label: Decision
options: seats each state has in the House

why.1: A census counts people, not weather.
why.2: Ocean depth is not measured by a census.

prompts.title: Absolute and relative distance
prompts.context: Two towns in the Rocky Mountains are 30 km apart in a straight line, but the road between them climbs over a pass and the drive takes 90 minutes. Two towns on the Great Plains are 60 km apart, and the drive takes 40 minutes (invented times for practice).
prompts.prompt: Compare the two pairs of towns in absolute distance and in relative distance.
checklist: Gives the absolute distance of both pairs
Gives the relative distance (travel time) of both pairs
Says which pair is closer by each measure

earns.answer: The mountain towns are closer in absolute distance, 30 km against 60 km, but the plains towns are closer in relative distance, because the drive between them takes 40 minutes while the mountain drive takes 90.
earns.why: It speaks of both pairs for both measures and says which is closer in each.

misses.answer: The mountain towns are closer together than the plains towns.
misses.why: That is only absolute distance; a compare of the two ideas needs the travel times too.

why.1: 60 km is farther than 30 km.
why.2: 30 km and 60 km are not equal.

why.1: 90 minutes is the longer trip.
why.2: Travel time differs, so one pair is closer.

prompts.title: Polders and possibilism
prompts.context: In the Netherlands, people have built dikes and pumped water off low land since the Middle Ages. The Flevoland polders, drained in the 1950s and 1960s, became a province with fields and towns in 1986.
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which the Flevoland polders support possibilism rather than environmental determinism.
checklist: States the degree first (to a high degree, for example)
Says what the environment limited: low land and the sea
Shows people's choice and technology changing that limit

earns.answer: To a high degree: the sea and the low land set limits, but the Dutch chose to build dikes and pumps and drained Flevoland in the 1950s and 1960s, so new fields and towns stand where there was water, which shows people working within the environment, not the land deciding for them.
earns.why: It states the degree first, then gives the limit and the choice that overcame it.

misses.answer: The Netherlands has a lot of water, and the Dutch built dikes along the coast.
misses.why: No degree is stated, and it never ties the dikes to possibilism or determinism.

why.1: Draining the sea for fields is strong evidence of human choice.
why.2: The polders are a clear case of people changing their options.

evidence.label: Evidence
options: dikes and pumps turned sea into fields
the climate decided where people live

why.1: That is determinism, the view the polders argue against.
why.2: Flevoland was drained and settled.

prompts.title: A limit of environmental determinism
prompts.prompt: Explain one limit of environmental determinism, using two named countries.
checklist: Says what environmental determinism claims
Names two real countries with very different climates
Explains why their similar ways of life weaken the claim

earns.answer: Environmental determinism says climate decides how people live, but Norway, cold and dark in winter, and Singapore, hot and wet all year, are both wealthy, high-tech countries with similar ways of life, so technology and people's choices shape their lives more than climate does.
earns.why: It states the claim, names two places and explains why they contradict it.

misses.answer: Environmental determinism is an old idea that is no longer accepted.
misses.why: True, but it gives no reason or example: a limit needs a case that the idea gets wrong.

why.1: That is possibilism, the view that replaced it.
why.2: That is not a claim of either view.

evidence.label: A case it gets wrong
options: Norway and Singapore: different climates, similar lives
two hot countries with similar lives
one cold country with a cold climate

why.1: Similar climates and lives would fit determinism.
why.2: One country cannot show a contrast.

prompts.title: Income at two scales
prompts.context: In the US Census Bureau's 2016-2020 five-year estimates, the median household income of McDowell County, West Virginia, was less than half the national median.
prompts.prompt: Explain how changing the scale of analysis changes what the income data show.
checklist: Names both scales: national and local
Says what each scale shows
Explains what the national figure hides

earns.answer: At the national scale, the United States looks wealthy, but at the local scale, McDowell County's median household income was less than half the national median (US Census Bureau, 2016-2020), so the national figure hides poorer places, and a planner choosing where to send help needs the local data.
earns.why: It names both scales and explains what the larger one hides.

misses.answer: McDowell County is poorer than most of the rest of the country.
misses.why: It states one fact but never names a scale or says how the picture changes between them.

why.1: Global data would compare countries.
why.2: That is the coarser scale here.

why.1: Income data say nothing about area.
why.2: The count of counties is not what the income figure shows.

prompts.title: Formal and functional regions
prompts.context: The Corn Belt of the US Midwest is known for wide fields of corn and soybeans. A newspaper delivers each morning to homes up to 80 km from its printing plant in Des Moines, Iowa (invented distance for practice).
prompts.prompt: Compare the Corn Belt and the newspaper's delivery area as kinds of regions.
checklist: Names the kind of region for both
Says what defines each: a shared trait, or links to a center
Speaks of both regions, not one alone

earns.answer: The Corn Belt is a formal region, defined by a shared trait across the whole area, wide fields of corn and soybeans, whereas the newspaper's delivery area is a functional region, defined by its links to one center, the printing plant in Des Moines.
earns.why: It names a kind for each and says what defines each one.

misses.answer: The Corn Belt is a formal region because it grows a lot of corn.
misses.why: One side only: a compare also says what kind of region the delivery area is and why.

why.1: Nothing in the Corn Belt is tied to one center.
why.2: It is defined by what grows there, not by feelings.

why.1: Homes in it share a link to the plant, not a trait.
why.2: It is set by deliveries from one place.

prompts.title: Describing where Egyptians live
prompts.prompt: Describe the pattern of population distribution in Egypt.
checklist: Says where people cluster, with named features
Says where few people live
Uses more than one word such as "clustered"

earns.answer: Egypt's people are clustered in a narrow strip along the Nile valley and in the Nile delta, around Cairo and Alexandria, while the deserts to the east and west, most of the country's land, are almost empty.
earns.why: It names where people are, where they are not and the features that mark the pattern.

misses.answer: Egypt's population is clustered near the river.
misses.why: "Clustered" alone earns little: it does not say where or around what.

pattern.label: Where people cluster
options: along the Nile valley and delta

why.1: Egypt's people are far from even: most of the land is empty.
why.2: The desert is the emptiest part.

why.1: Egypt does not touch the Indian Ocean.
why.2: The Sahara is the desert, almost empty.

prompts.title: Why physiological density fits Egypt
prompts.prompt: Explain why physiological density shows the pressure on Egypt's farmland better than arithmetic density.
checklist: Says what each density divides by
Notes that most of Egypt cannot grow crops
Links that to what physiological density reveals

earns.answer: Most of Egypt is desert that cannot grow crops, so arithmetic density spreads people over land where no one grows crops; physiological density divides people by arable land only, so it shows how many people each square kilometer of farmland must feed, which is very high along the Nile.
earns.why: It says what each measure divides by and links the desert to the gap between them.

misses.answer: Physiological density is people per unit of farmland.
misses.why: A definition, not an explanation: it never says why the measure fits Egypt.

why.1: That is arithmetic density.
why.2: Farmers over farmland is agricultural density.

cause.label: Why it fits Egypt
options: Egypt's people live in the desert

why.1: Egypt has one great river, the Nile.
why.2: Almost no one lives in the desert.

prompts.title: Comparing two pyramids
prompts.context: In the UN's 2024 estimates (World Population Prospects 2024), Niger's population pyramid is widest at the base, and Japan's is narrow at the base with its widest bands in middle and older age.
prompts.prompt: Compare the population pyramids of Niger and Japan and what each says about growth.
checklist: Names the shape of both pyramids
Says what each shape means for growth
Speaks of both countries, not one alone

earns.answer: Niger's pyramid is expansive, with a wide base of children and a narrow top, whereas Japan's is constrictive, with a narrow base and wide bands of older adults, so Niger's population is young and growing fast while Japan's is aging and shrinking.
earns.why: It names both shapes and what each means, side by side.

misses.answer: Niger's pyramid has a wide base because it has many children.
misses.why: Only one side: a compare must also say what Japan's pyramid shows.

sideA.label: Niger
options: expansive: a wide base, growing fast

why.1: Niger's base is wide, not narrow.
why.2: Niger's sides narrow quickly toward the top.

why.1: Japan's base is narrow.
why.2: Japan's population is shrinking.

prompts.title: How well Country B fits the model
prompts.context: Invented Country B's crude death rate fell from 25 to 8 per 1,000 between 1950 and 1990; its crude birth rate stayed near 45 until 1970, then fell to 15 by 2020 (invented data for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which Country B's data are consistent with the demographic transition model.
checklist: States the degree first: to a high degree, for example
Uses the order of the changes: deaths fell first, then births
Says what the model does not explain

earns.answer: To a high degree: Country B's death rate fell first, from 25 to 8 per 1,000, while its birth rate stayed near 45, and then births fell to 15, which is the order the model's stages 2 and 3 predict. The model says less about why births fell when they did.
earns.why: It states the degree, uses the data in order and names what the model leaves out.

misses.answer: Country B is in stage 3 of the demographic transition.
misses.why: No degree, no data, and it states a stage as a fact: say the data are consistent with a stage.

why.1: The order of the changes matches the model closely.
why.2: Deaths falling before births is the model's core pattern.

why.1: Both fell in these data.
why.2: Here deaths fell first.

prompts.title: A limit of Malthus
prompts.context: Malthus wrote in 1798 that population grows faster than food. World population grew from about 1 billion around 1800 to about 8.2 billion in 2024 (UN WPP 2024).
prompts.prompt: Explain one limit of Malthusian theory, using what happened after 1800.
checklist: Says what Malthus predicted
Says what happened instead
Explains why: food output grew faster than he expected

earns.answer: Malthus predicted that population would outgrow food and bring famine, but world population grew about eightfold after 1800 while food supply per person rose, because farmers learned to grow far more food on the same land, so his theory underestimated technology.
earns.why: It states the prediction, what happened and why the theory missed it.

misses.answer: Malthus was wrong because there are more people now.
misses.why: More people alone does not show a limit: the point is that food kept up.

why.1: That is the opposite of his claim.
why.2: He made no such forecast.

limit.label: What he missed
options: farmers grew far more food on the same land
the world ran out of land

why.1: Population kept growing after 1800.
why.2: Output rose without needing far more land.

prompts.title: Naming a pronatalist policy
prompts.context: A student writes: "Some governments reward families for having more children."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim so it names a real country, the policy and the year it began.
checklist: Names a real country, not a region or continent
Names the policy and when it began
Says what the policy is meant to do

earns.answer: In Hungary, since 2020, mothers who have raised four or more children pay no personal income tax, a pronatalist policy meant to raise the birth rate; the government widened it to mothers of three in 2025 and to younger mothers of two in 2026.
earns.why: It names the country, the year, the policy and its aim.

misses.answer: Some countries, like ones in Europe, pay families to have more children.
misses.why: "Ones in Europe" names no country, and no policy or year is given.

why.1: Europe is a continent, not a country.
why.2: That names no country.

why.1: A tax break for mothers encourages births.
why.2: The policy is about births, not migration.

prompts.title: Aging at two scales in China
prompts.context: China's population is aging. Since the 1980s, many young adults have moved from rural villages to work in factories on the coast.
prompts.prompt: Explain how the age structure of China's population looks different at the national and local scales.
checklist: Names both scales of analysis: national and local
Says what each scale shows about age
Explains the cause of the difference: young adults moving away for work

earns.answer: At the national scale, China is aging, but at the local scale, many rural villages have a much older population than the coast, because young adults left to work in coastal factories and older people stayed behind, so the villages age faster than the country as a whole.
earns.why: It names both scales, says what each shows and gives the cause.

misses.answer: China has an aging population because people have fewer children.
misses.why: True at the national scale, but it says nothing about the other scale the prompt asks for.

scale.label: The finer scale
options: the local scale: villages and towns

why.1: Global data compare countries, not villages.
why.2: That is the coarser scale.

cause.label: Why villages are older
options: young adults left for factory jobs
older people moved to the villages

why.1: Most moves ran from villages to the coast, by the young.
why.2: More babies would make villages younger.

prompts.title: Reading a fertility legend
prompts.context: A world map shades countries by total fertility rate in four classes: under 1.5, 1.5 to under 2.1, 2.1 to under 3.0, and 3.0 or more children per woman (invented values for practice).
prompts.prompt: Explain what being in the 1.5 to under 2.1 class suggests about a country's future population.
checklist: Reads the class: below about 2.1 children per woman
Ties it to replacement level
Explains the effect over time, without migration

earns.answer: A country in the 1.5 to under 2.1 class has a total fertility rate below 2.1, about the replacement level where deaths are low, so each generation is smaller than the one before, and without migration its population will age and eventually shrink.
earns.why: It reads the class, links it to replacement level and explains the effect.

misses.answer: Women in that country have about two children.
misses.why: It restates the class roughly but never explains what it means for the population.

data.label: The class
options: below the replacement level of about 2.1

why.1: The class tops out at 2.0, below 2.1.
why.2: A class is a range of averages, not each woman.

why.1: Fast growth needs fertility well above replacement.
why.2: Below-replacement fertility changes the population over time.

prompts.title: An economic push factor
prompts.context: Millions of people have left Venezuela since about 2015 (UNHCR, 2024).
prompts.prompt: Explain one economic push factor behind this migration.
checklist: Names an economic condition in Venezuela
Links it to people's daily lives
Ends at the decision to leave

earns.answer: Venezuela's economy collapsed after about 2014, with very high inflation and shortages of food and medicine, so wages could no longer buy enough food, and many families left to find work and goods elsewhere: an economic push factor.
earns.why: It names the condition and links it, step by step, to leaving.

misses.answer: Venezuela has economic problems, which is a push factor.
misses.why: It names a push factor but never says how the problems made people leave.

why.1: Climate did not change; the economy did.
why.2: Jobs abroad are a pull factor, not a push.

link.label: Link
options: so wages could not buy enough food
so families earned more at home

why.1: Wages lost their value.
why.2: Prices rose sharply.

prompts.title: What remittance figures miss
prompts.context: The World Bank publishes yearly figures for remittances, the money migrants send home, counted through banks and money transfer firms.
prompts.prompt: Explain one limitation of these figures.
checklist: Names what the figures leave out
Explains why it is left out
Says which way the figures are off

earns.answer: The figures count only money sent through formal channels, such as banks and transfer companies, so cash carried home by travelers or sent informally is missed, and the true flow is likely larger than the figures show.
earns.why: It names what is missed, why, and the direction of the error.

misses.answer: The data could be old or wrong, so they might not be accurate.
misses.why: Too vague: it names no specific gap in what the figures count.

limit.label: What is missed
options: money sent informally or carried as cash

why.1: Bank transfers are what the figures count.
why.2: Countries of origin are in the data.

effect.label: Effect
options: the true flow is likely larger

why.1: Missing money makes the count too low, not too high.
why.2: Missing flows mean the figures are not exact.

prompts.title: Describing a cultural landscape
prompts.prompt: Describe how the entrance and streets of San Francisco's Chinatown show its cultural landscape.
checklist: Names a specific feature, with where it is
Says what it looks like and what culture it shows
Goes beyond naming the neighborhood

earns.answer: The Dragon Gate on Grant Avenue, built in 1970, marks the entrance to Chinatown with a Chinese-style tiled roof and dragons, and the streets behind it have signs in Chinese and English and shops selling Chinese food and goods.
earns.why: It names features, says what they look like and ties them to a culture.

misses.answer: Chinatown in San Francisco has a Chinese cultural landscape.
misses.why: It names the place but describes no feature of the landscape.

evidence.label: A feature
options: the Dragon Gate on Grant Avenue

why.1: The bridge is not in Chinatown.
why.2: The ocean is physical geography, not a cultural feature.

concept.label: What it shows
options: Chinese culture written on the landscape
the physical landscape of the bay

why.1: A gate and signs are built by people: cultural, not physical.
why.2: Climate is not shown by a gate.

prompts.title: Why Canada has two official languages
prompts.context: Canada's Official Languages Act of 1969 made English and French its official languages.
prompts.prompt: Explain why Canada has two official languages.
checklist: Names where French speakers are concentrated
Links that population pattern to the 1969 law
Says what the law does for both groups

earns.answer: Canada has a large French-speaking population, mostly in Quebec, as well as an English-speaking majority, so the 1969 Official Languages Act made both official, which means federal services reach each group in its own language.
earns.why: It names the pattern, links it to the law and says what the law does.

misses.answer: Canada has two official languages because of a law passed in 1969.
misses.why: The law is the result, not the reason: it never says why the law was passed.

cause.label: Pattern
